label: text

CENTENARY OF LADY
ANNE BARNARD

label: text
text: A hundred years ago (on May 6) died Lady Anne Bargard, the authoress of the Scottish ballad, "Auld Robin Gray." She was a daughter of James Lindsay, fifth Earl of Balcarres, and was born on December 8, 1750. When she was forty-three she married Mr. Andrew Barnard, a son of the Bishop of Limerick, and accompanied her husband to South Africa in 1793, when he was appointed secretary to the colony of the Cape of Good Hope under Lord Macartney. Returning to England in 1802, she resided in London until her death on May 6, 1825, at the age of seventy-five.

label: text
text: Lady Anne Lindsay was a vivacious young woman of twenty-one when she composed her famous ballad in the ancestral hall of the Lindsay, old Balcarres House, near Colinsburgh, in the East of Fife. The ballad was written to suit an ancient Scottish melody of which Lady Anne was very fond; but soon after its publication a new air for it was composed by an English clergyman, the Rev. Mr. Leoves, rector of Wrington, Somersetshire: It is to the English tune that the ballad has been mostly sung.

label: text
text: The secret of the authorship was kept for more than half a century. Lady Anne revealed it only in 1823 in a letter to Sir Walter Scott. In the year of Lady Anne's death, Sir Walter Scott edited the ballad for the Bannatyne Club, with several additions, which, however, are poor. Lady Anne herself had written two additions to the original version.

label: text
text: Lady Anne wrote other poems, none of which are remembered, and some of her prose is preserve. In the pages of "The Lives of the Lindsay's."

label: text
text: WOMAN GOVERNOR PARDONS HUSBAND

label: text
text: "Ma Ferguson will pardon I'm Ferguson!" This message from Texas indicates that Mr. Miriam Ferguson, the woman Governor of Texas, will support legislation granting a full amnesty to her husband, who was ousted from the office of Governor some years ago on impeachment proceedings charging him with malveration of public funds. The question of the validity of the proposed amnesty will be contested in both Houses of the Texas legislature, but the chances are that Mrs. Ferguson will win the seven-year fight to free her husband's name from the stigma attaching to it, albeit the former Governor, judging from the despatches, seems to be almost as influential with his wife as Governor as when he himself held the reins of the State Executive. Mr. Ferguson himself always alleged that he was the victim of political unscrupulousness. Both the Forgusons are bitter enemies of the Ku-Klux Klan, and to that organisation the husband attributed the failure of his campaign to enter the race for the Presidency of the United States on the Texas Republican ticket. This was two years after he had been removed from office and Texas had refused to re-elect him Governor.

label: text
text: This question was debated by Miss Rebecca West, the novelist, and Mr. Alfred Duff Cooper, M.P. (Con., Oldham), at the London School of Economics, Clare-market, Lincoln's In-fields. So controversial was the reasoning that people who had gone to help the King Edward's Hospital Fund—in aid of which the debate had been arranged—went away debating the question themselves.

label: text
text: Miss West declared that men are in some ways becoming more like women, and added:

label: text
text: I have known men, quite often, so feminine that they wanted to wear the skirt, but I have never come across a woman who wanted to wear two skirts—which is practically what the Oxford trousers are. (Loud laughter.)

label: text
text: In past ages men did a great deal of useful work and showed initiative and. courage. But man's present-day sense is at war with his primitive sense, and he has become excitable and hysterical. (Laughter.)

label: text
text: If men want to go back to the home we should be sympathetic. Men have been running the world for centuries, but woman is seen to be a more satisfactory article. (Laughter.)

label: text
text: Mr. Cooper said that if the wearing of two skirts were given as proof of femininity one had only to remember the hobble skirt, which almost prevented women from walking at all.

label: text
text: Women's function was that of rearing children. Were women ashamed of that natural function? It was a tremendous thing for her to see that the meals were properly cooked. Woman was ruler of the kitchen as of the nursery, and also displayed the art of entertaining in the drawingroom.

label: paragraph_title
text: GIRL'S DEATH.

label: paragraph_title
text: CORONER'S QUESTIONS TO FATHER.

label: paragraph_title
text: DENIALS OF CRUELTY.

label: text
text: At an inquest at Westminster on Ellen Jackson, 13, who was found drowned in the Thames, James Jackson, the father, a steel worker, of Latchmere-grove, Battersea, said his wife died on March 6, and since then "the girl had been " trying to run the house." There were four other children at home. Ellen had been going to school every day and the children had their meals at a relative's house.

label: text
text: The Coroner (Mr. Oddie): Can you explain why this girl should drown herself?—No, except worry. There was something else for

label: text
text: her to worry about, wasn't there?—I smacked her because she had only a few shillings left out of £3 or £4 I had given her. She had paid the rent and 12s. 6d. for the children's food.

label: text
text: It was not the only time you have hit her?—Never before that. That is not my information. You have thrashed her frequently and without sufficient cause?—No.

label: text
text: Did you ever threaten to kill her?—No.

label: text
text: Didn't you flog her on Thursday [the day before she disappeared]? —No.

label: text
text: I am told that you used to knock your wife about. What do you say to that?—That is a direct lie.

label: text
text: Jackson said that he only hit the girl with his flat hand on the face.

label: text
text: The Coroner: Why did you do that? She had already got enough trouble, having lost her mother and being left at the age of thirteen in charge of the household. Wasn't it a brutal thing to do? She is dead now, you know, and that is the cause of it. That will do.

label: text
text: Sergt. Nichols, the coroner's officer, said he was informed that before his wife died Jackson was a confirmed wife beater and a very heavy drinker; that on one occasion, when the father had threatened to kill all the children, the girl said she would drown herself, and then few days before her death, when her father was shouting and raving, the girl appeared obviously terrorised.

label: text
text: The coroner said he must have some substantiation of those statements and adjourned the inquiry.

label: text
text: HOW A SICK MAN WAS

label: text

Mr. William Harvey, F.S.A.
Scot, gave a talk from Dundee
Wireless Station and told many

label: text
text: An old carter in a' certain village had a rare fund of eloquence, and the children used to gather round him for the sheer delight of hearing his lurid language.

label: text
text: One day Jamie was driving a cart of sand up a very steep hill, when some mischievous bairns, seeing their opportunity, slipped up behind, knocked the tailboard out of the cart, and then, taking a near road, reached the top of the hill to hear what Jamie would say when he arrived there.

label: text
text: When the cart got to the top Jamie drew rein, filled his pipe, and then sauntered round the cart to see that everything was in order. When he got to the back, and beheld what had taken place, his eyes passed from the empty cart to the expectant children, and he said, "Run awa'hame, laddies; run awa'hame. I'm no' equal to the occasion."

label: text
text: A workman went home feeling very far from well, and his wife bundled him into bed and sent for the doctor. After an examination, the doctor told the wife that her husband was very ill, and instructed her to take his temperature during the night, intimidating that he would be back in the morning.

label: text
text: When the doctor returned next day, expecting to sign the man's death certificate, Macdonald was sitting up in bed smoking a short cutty pipe, and belching forth great clouds of black smoke.

label: text
text: “Dear me,” said the doctor, “this is a very wonderful recovery. What have you done to him?”

label: text
text: "Weel, sir," explained the wife, "you telled me to tak' his temperature. We dinna ha'e a thermometer, but the wife—up—the stair has a barometer and she gled me a len' o' it. I put it on his breast just below the blankets, and when I looked at it in about ten minutes the lang hand was pointin' to 'Very dry,' so I just gled him two glass o' whusky and a bottle o' beer—and there he is."

label: text
text: An old Scot called upon the local Registrar one afternoon and said he wished to register the death of his wife.

label: text
text: "I'm sorry to hear that; I didn't know that Mrs. Robertson was ill. When did she die?" said the Registrar.

label: text
text:
"Oh, she's no' deed yet," ex
plained the husband.

label: text
text: "But you can't register a death before it takes place," was the reply.

label: text
text: "Can you 'no'?" queried the man. "Man, I'm sorry about that. I'll be busy the morn, and I thocht if I could have dune it this afternoon it would save time. You see, the doctor says she canna live over the nicht and he kens what he's gien her!"
